description:
It’s getting cold outside, so let’s make something that tastes like Christmas in a scoop — Gingerbread Cookie Dough Ice Cream.

This recipe builds a 12% fat custard base balanced with glucose syrup, molasses, and warm spices. We’ll dive into the science behind fat crystallization, spice oil solubility, and freezing point depression — then fold in soft, edible gingerbread dough for texture and contrast.

No no-churn shortcuts here — this is a true Polar Ice Creamery recipe: rich, balanced, and scientifically designed for the perfect creamy scoop at –18°C.
---------

Ingredients for the base:
458g milk 3.25% (1.75 cups)
264g cream 33-35% (1 cup)
65g egg yolk (0.25 cups)
115g sugar (0.5 cups)
17g glucose or corn syrup (1.25 tbsp)
45g SMP (2.5 tbsp)
26g molasses 1.75 tbsp)
6 g ground ginger (1 tsp)
4g cinnamon (0.75 tsp)
1g nutmeg (0.25 tsp)
0.5g ground cloves (large pinch)
1g salt (large pinch)
10g vanilla extract (2 tsp)

The Gingerbread Cookie Dough:
Heat-treated flour 100g (0.5 cups + 2 tbsp)
Soft butter 40g (3 tbsp)
Brown sugar 50g (0.25 cups)
Molasses 25g (1.75 tbsp)
Milk 10g (2 tsp)
Ground ginger 2g (0.5 tsp)
Cinnamon 1g (0.25 tsp)
Nutmeg 0.3g (large pinch)
Clove (optional) 0.1g (large pinch)
Salt 0.5g (pinch)
Vanilla extract 2g or as much or as little as you want (0.5 tsp-2 tsp)

Maker: Lello Musso
I made this delicious Ice Cream! I have to say it was a great recipe, although technical. I did find that the Cookie Dough and Ice Cream clashed a little, and thought that the Cookie Dough would be better in a custard mix, however the overall result was excellent. I also like to make an egg based recipe sometimes, as it takes on a thicker, heavier texture in comparison to no egg. It's worth saying that the superstar is the spice mix, and the smell. It tastes and smells like Christmas oil every bite!

Overall, this one is definitely recommended. Nicks recipes, and demonstrations ,are second to none!

comments.text: Ello! I wonder if icecream circle's ever used (freeze) distilled milk for the ice cream base? Especially in bases that aren't heated during mixing. Milk tea industry and baristas uses these types of milk a lot - high-end milk tea shops uses the only brand that makes these en masse as their milk base, and baristas call this competition milk because they bring their own to competitions.  I think the only company in questions that mass produces them has vendors in Europe. Want to know your expert's opinion on this matter. Distilled (technically it's condensation but w/e) milk tastes really really salty+sweet and cream-cheesy as it concentrates the non-cream part of the flavor, so it's more than just a half-and-half. It's also rather easy to make at home - you just freeze the milk solid and thaw it out in fractions or continuously -  but without a good thawing setup the consistency of the product will vary each batch.
